idiom_name: Django signed_cookies session backend - a MAC-signed session in a single cookie
implementation_notes: Django ships the pattern as a session backend: setting SESSION_ENGINE to django.contrib.sessions.backends.signed_cookies makes request.session be serialized, compressed, signed with SECRET_KEY and stored in the session cookie, with no server-side record written at all; the same request.session API then works exactly as with a database store, so the choice is a settings change. Set SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY (Django recommends True), SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE and SESSION_COOKIE_AGE deliberately, and respect the backend's two documented limits: the data is signed but not encrypted, and there is no freshness guarantee, so logout does not invalidate a stolen cookie. When the payload approaches the 4096-byte cookie limit or must stay confidential, switch SESSION_ENGINE to cached_db or cache rather than bolting encryption onto the cookie.
code_sketch:
# settings.py
SESSION_ENGINE = "django.contrib.sessions.backends.signed_cookies"
SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY = True
SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = True
SESSION_COOKIE_AGE = 1800

# views.py
def add_to_cart(request, sku):
    request.session.setdefault("items", []).append(sku)   # rewritten as a signed cookie
    return JsonResponse({"items": request.session["items"]})
pitfalls: Signed but not encrypted: the session payload is readable by the client, so PII and internal identifiers leak by default.
Cookie sessions are not invalidated on logout and carry no freshness guarantee, so a stolen cookie stays usable until SESSION_COOKIE_AGE - use a server-side backend when revocation matters.
The client can drop the cookie data - it is only a cookie - and because the MAC covers the dropped bytes the whole session is invalidated; Django also documents the 4096-byte limit behind this.
Rotating or per-process generating SECRET_KEY invalidates every live session, a common accident in multi-instance deployments.
